title: A variance inflation factor says how well one input can be rebuilt from the others, and two red bars here say two inputs are nearly the same
summary: The left panel is a correlation matrix of the candidate inputs and the target; the right panel converts the same information into one number per input, the variance inflation factor (VIF). Two inputs sit far beyond the usual threshold of 10, so the check does not confirm that the inputs are non-redundant.

media.alt: Two panels titled Collinearity Diagnostics. Left: lower-triangular Pearson correlation matrix for nine variables, with values printed. Strong dark red cells link BDE of the broken bond, BDE squared and the activation energy, with correlations of 0.98 to 0.99, and the reaction enthalpy at 0.80 to 0.84. Right: horizontal bar chart of variance inflation factors, with dashed vertical lines at 5 (orange) and 10 (red). BDE squared is about 44 and BDE of the broken bond about 39, both red; reaction enthalpy about 4.5; the other five bars between 1 and 2, all green.

source.caption: Feature collinearity / VIF check
source.note: Single-figure group. The page describes it as confirming the inputs are not redundant; the figure shows two inputs with VIF far above 10. Only the generic VIF reading is taught; no fitted rate rule is described.
group: 01_01_collinearity: Feature collinearity / VIF check (the only figure in this group)
source.project_title: Symbolic Regression for Universal Rate Rules

read_the_figure.question: Are the inputs offered to the regression independent enough that their individual effects can be told apart?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: the same nine variables on both axes (eight candidate inputs and the target Ea, in kcal/mol); each cell is a Pearson correlation between the row and column variable, on a colour scale from -1 (blue) to +1 (red); only the lower triangle is shown. Right: one bar per input, the variance inflation factor (dimensionless, 1 is the minimum), with dashed guide lines at 5 (orange) and 10 (red). Bars are coloured green below 5-ish and red above 10.
look_at: In the left panel, find the dark red block: BDE of the broken bond, its square (BDE_sq) and the target Ea correlate at 0.98 to 0.99 with each other. The reaction enthalpy is at 0.80 to 0.84 with those three.
In the right panel, read the two red bars: BDE_sq about 44 and BDE of the broken bond about 39, both far to the right of the red line at 10.
The reaction enthalpy bar is at about 4.5, just under the orange line at 5. The other five inputs are between 1 and 2: effectively independent.
The target Ea is in the correlation matrix but not in the VIF panel: VIF is computed among inputs only.
read_the_figure.proves: That most inputs are nearly independent of each other, and that two inputs (the bond dissociation energy and its square) are strongly redundant. It does not say whether they should be dropped.
if_wrong: A VIF above 10 means more than 90 percent of that input's variance can be reproduced from the other inputs: its coefficient in a linear model has a variance inflated by at least that factor.
A correlation of 0.99 between an input and the target is not a problem of redundancy among inputs: it is a strong, nearly linear relation the model should capture.
A feature and its own square are almost always correlated when the feature does not range over both signs; centring the feature reduces this.
must_check: VIF is computed among the inputs only and on the same data used for the fit.
Thresholds are drawn and justified (5 and 10 are conventions, not laws).
The sample size is given: not printed here.
Derived inputs (squares, products) are flagged, because they are collinear with their parents by construction.
A decision is stated: keep, drop, centre or combine.
as_drawn: VIF values read off the right panel by eye: BDE_sq about 44, BDE (broken bond) about 39, reaction enthalpy about 4.5, nitrogen count about 1.9, radical site about 1.7, bond-broken encoding about 1.5, carbon count about 1.5, ring strain about 1.1.
Printed correlations: BDE with Ea 0.99, BDE_sq with Ea 0.98, BDE with BDE_sq 0.98, BDE with reaction enthalpy 0.80, BDE_sq with reaction enthalpy 0.84, Ea with reaction enthalpy 0.81.
A VIF of 39 corresponds to R squared = 1 - 1/39, about 0.974 of the variance of that input explained by the others (computed).

terms.meaning: Two or more inputs that are nearly linear functions of each other. Their separate effects cannot be told apart from the data.
A symmetric table of linear correlations between every pair of variables. Colour encodes sign and strength.
For input j, how many times larger the variance of its estimated coefficient is than it would be if j were uncorrelated with the other inputs.
The fraction of input j's variance explained by a linear regression on all the other inputs.
A feature computed from another, such as BDE squared. It is collinear with its parent unless the parent is centred.
A search over mathematical expressions to fit data. Correlated inputs make several different expressions equally good, so the one found is partly arbitrary.
A conventional line (here VIF of 5 and of 10) above which collinearity is considered a concern.

remember: VIF_j = 1 / (1 - R_j^2): VIF 5 means R_j^2 = 0.8, VIF 10 means 0.9.
VIF is the diagonal of the inverse of the correlation matrix of the inputs.
A feature and its square are collinear by construction unless the feature is centred.
Collinearity does not damage prediction inside the data range; it damages the interpretation of individual terms.
The thresholds 5 and 10 are conventions: state which one you apply.

understand.title: From the matrix to the bar
understand.text: The correlation matrix shows pairs; VIF asks a stronger question: can this input be rebuilt from all the others together? A VIF can be large even when no single pairwise correlation is, because several inputs together can reproduce one. That is why the bars are the more reliable summary.

understand.title: Why BDE and BDE squared are red
understand.text: The energy ranges over positive values only, so its square rises with it almost along a straight line: correlation 0.98. Putting both in the model offers the search two names for nearly the same quantity. The enthalpy is correlated at 0.8 to 0.84 with both, which adds to their VIF but keeps its own at about 4.5.

understand.title: What the check does and does not support
understand.text: The panel supports 'the other five inputs are independent of each other'. It does not support 'no input is redundant': it shows two that are. It is also silent about the target: an input can have a VIF of 1 and still be useless for predicting Ea.

steps.title: Regress one input on the rest
steps.note: The auxiliary regression for input j. R squared says how much of x_j the other inputs reproduce.

steps.title: Definition of VIF
steps.note: Equals 1 when x_j is orthogonal to the rest and grows without bound as R squared approaches 1.

steps.title: Where the name comes from
steps.note: In ordinary least squares the variance of the estimated coefficient is inflated by exactly the VIF compared with uncorrelated inputs.

steps.title: Shortcut from the correlation matrix
steps.note: The VIFs are the diagonal of the inverse of the inputs' correlation matrix, so no separate regressions are needed.

steps.title: Two inputs only
steps.note: With just two inputs R squared equals r squared. For r = 0.98 the VIF is about 25. The red bars here are larger (about 39 and 44) because further inputs, notably the reaction enthalpy, add to the redundancy.

steps.title: Thresholds in terms of R squared
steps.note: The two dashed lines are those two levels of redundancy.

steps.title: Why centring helps for squares
steps.tex: x\to x-\bar x:\quad \mathrm{Corr}(x-\bar x,\,(x-\bar x)^{2})\approx 0\ \text{for a symmetric spread}
steps.note: After centring, a symmetric variable and its square are uncorrelated, so the derived feature stops duplicating its parent. Valid for a roughly symmetric distribution.

worked.title: How redundant is an input with VIF 39?
worked.problem: The bar for BDE of the broken bond reads about 39. What fraction of its variance do the other inputs explain, and by how much is the variance of its coefficient inflated?

solution.text: The variance inflation is the VIF itself, so the coefficient's standard error is inflated by its square root.

worked.answer: About 97 percent of the input is rebuilt from the others and the coefficient's standard error is about 6 times larger than for an independent input.

analyze.q: Ea correlates 0.99 with the bond dissociation energy. Is that collinearity in the sense of the right panel? What does it mean for the regression?
analyze.hint: VIF uses inputs only; a strong input-target relation is the thing you want.

analyze.q: The reaction enthalpy has a VIF of about 4.5, below 5, yet it correlates 0.8 to 0.84 with two red inputs. Why is its VIF so much lower than theirs?
analyze.hint: Which part of its variance do the others not reproduce?

analyze.q: List the three consequences of keeping both BDE and BDE_sq in a symbolic-regression search.
analyze.hint: Duplicate expressions, unstable terms, arbitrary choice.

evaluate.q: The page says this figure confirms the inputs are not redundant. Is that what it shows? Write the sentence you would put in the caption instead.
Decide: drop BDE_sq, centre BDE, or keep both? Give the one measurement that would support your choice.
evaluate.hint: Re-computing VIF after the change is the check.

create: Redraw the right panel with VIFs recomputed after centring BDE, and a note on the decision.
Add a third panel that shows, for each input, its correlation with Ea, so that redundancy among inputs and relevance to the target are read together.

checks.q: What does a VIF of 1 mean?
checks.hint: R squared of the auxiliary regression.
checks.answer: The input is uncorrelated with the others (R_j^2 = 0): its coefficient is not inflated at all.

checks.q: An input has R_j^2 = 0.9. What is its VIF?
Why does BDE squared have such a high VIF?
checks.answer: BDE is positive over its whole range, so its square increases with it almost linearly; the two are nearly the same information (correlation 0.98).
By the common thresholds of 5 and 10 it is below both lines, so usually acceptable, but it is close to 5 and should be re-checked if the inputs change.

checks.q: How would you remove the collinearity between a feature and its square without dropping either?
checks.answer: Subtract the mean from the feature before squaring (centring), or use orthogonal polynomial terms. Recompute the VIF to check.
